art.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news runs from your own valley to Paris, London and New York, with a good deal of painting, performance and storytelling mixed in.

Let me begin close to home. The Musée de Grenoble is showing an exhibition on Anne Truitt, called Libérer la couleur, or Freeing Colour. The listing I have gives only the title, but that is enough to suggest a show built around her work with colour, and it is on your doorstep. Also in the city, Arts in the City points to the Place de Gordes, where calligraphy has appeared as a public art intervention, according to l'Essentiel. I only have the headline, so I can't tell you who is behind it, but it may be worth a short detour on a walk through town. Just outside Grenoble, in Fontaine, there is an exhibition from the Atelier Eugénie Fauny. The listing on jds.fr gives dates, hours and prices, but my text carries only the title, so do check it before you set off. And for a mountain theme, Le Dauphiné Libéré recommends an exhibition called Encordés, about the pioneers of mountaineering, past and present. I don't have a venue or dates, but with Belledonne outside your window, it feels made for you.

Now to the conversations between painting and the other arts. Radio France has a lovely small idea: it asks listeners what music they hear in Vilhelm Hammershøi's painting "Paysage de Lejre". The piece is brief, but the question is a good one to put to a quiet Danish landscape, and perhaps to a class too. What would your seconde pupils hear?

On the stage, Beaux Arts Magazine reports that at the Théâtre Montparnasse in Paris, the great Catherine Hiegel plays the painter Suzanne Valadon. The play is set in 1935, three years before Valadon's death, so it looks at an artist late in life, looking back. Further south, the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nice is offering guided visits to its exhibition "De la scène à la toile", from stage to canvas. The listing gives no dates, but the title tells you the theme: how performance finds its way into painting.

In Paris again, the Musée Gustave Moreau is giving a carte blanche to the contemporary painter Ali Banisadr, in a show called Talisman. The idea is that he responds to Moreau's world. Moreau's Symbolist paintings are so close to myth and literature that the pairing seems promising. The text I have gives no dates, so do check the full listing.

On the literary side, there is a Front Row episode from BBC Radio 4, forty-two minutes long, in which the thriller writer Karin Slaughter talks about adapting her novel The Good Daughter for television. The story is set in her native Georgia, and she discusses what changes when a page-turner moves to the screen. The same programme also includes a segment on a Norwich exhibition about the kiss in art, so you get a thriller and a bit of art history in one listen.

Next, a few pieces about the lives behind the art. The National Gallery has published a three-part film series called Linked Lives: Art and Empire. It looks at how the gallery's early history was shaped by empire and colonialism, and it draws on Dr Sean Cham's research into the people behind the paintings, including enslaved people who are often left out of institutional history. It could be useful for anyone teaching how a painting can carry a hidden story. Hyperallergic, meanwhile, reviews a new documentary on the collage artist Romare Bearden. The reviewer finds its best moments in simply watching people engage with his work, which suits an artist whose pictures are built from fragments. And The Guardian has a piece on a new travelogue with a wonderful title, With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna. It explores queer subcultures in Budapest, Prague and other central European cities, and challenges the region's reputation for illiberalism. It touches on language, on Wittgenstein, and on an art exhibition about masculinity. The headline quotes a line that homosexuality was coined by a Hungarian, which tells you something of the book's playful, questioning spirit.

Finally, photography, and The Guardian is rich in it today. There is a profile of Jill Posener, whose witty, feminist photographs of the nineteen-eighties answered misogyny and Thatcherite conservatism. Among them is a graffitied billboard she photographed on London's Farringdon Road in 1979. A retrospective now marks fifty years of her work, and the article is carried by her own words. She says she railed against the stereotype of the humourless lesbian, and she used humour as her weapon. A very different gallery shows Colin McPherson's project Catching the Tide, a portrait of Scotland's salmon fishers and of a way of life that is disappearing. It is a gallery of pictures rather than a long read, so it is one to look at slowly. And at the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York, a show called A Long Shadow runs until the second of May next year. It brings together fifteen artists, with prints, books, magazines and a video installation, to show how Japanese photographers documented postwar Japan. The Guardian notes that it is the first show of Japanese photography at the Met in over thirty years.

That is the round-up for today, Yamuna, and I hope something in it sends you out into the cold with a good reason to look at a picture.
art.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's art news has a pleasing shape: some colour and calligraphy close to home, a good run of paintings talking to theatre, music and literature, and a few stories about the lives behind the pictures.

Let me start in Grenoble. The Musée de Grenoble is showing an exhibition on Anne Truitt, called Libérer la couleur, or Freeing Colour. The report I have gives only the title, so I can't tell you what is in the rooms or how long it runs, but the title is a thoughtful one. It suggests colour treated not as decoration but as something to be set loose and allowed to be the subject. If you're planning a visit, the museum's own page will have the dates and hours.

Still in the city, l'Essentiel reports that calligraphy has appeared on the Place de Gordes in Grenoble. Again, the detail is slim, just the headline, but there is something lovely in the idea of handwriting, the line of a pen made large, turning up in an ordinary square. For someone who loves language as sound and shape, it may be worth a small detour the next time you are down in town.

A little further out, in Fontaine, there is an exhibition from the Atelier Eugénie Fauny. The listing on jds.fr carries the dates, opening hours and prices, though all I have is the title line, so I would look at the full page before setting off. It is the kind of small local show that suits a Saturday morning with a market stop on the way.

And closer to your own mountains, Le Dauphiné Libéré recommends an exhibition called Encordés, which it describes as a gripping epic of the pioneers of mountaineering, then and now. The report doesn't give a venue or dates, so I can't say where to find it. But anyone who lives under Belledonne will know there is a particular pleasure in seeing the history of climbing, the ropes, the nerve, the stories, set out on a wall. Mountaineering has also produced some memorable first-person writing, so it could make a good companion to a bit of reading.

Now to the paintings that seem to lean towards other arts. Let's begin in Paris, at the Musée Gustave Moreau, where a show called Talisman gives a carte blanche to the contemporary painter Ali Banisadr. The idea is that he responds to the world of the museum, and that is an intriguing invitation, because Moreau's Symbolist work already sits very close to literature, full of myth and dream and story. A living painter answering that world is a conversation across time. The listing I have, from jds.fr, doesn't give dates, so do check the full details if you are likely to be in Paris.

Also in Paris, but on stage, Beaux Arts Magazine writes about a play at the Théâtre Montparnasse in which the great Catherine Hiegel brings the painter Suzanne Valadon to life. The play is set in nineteen thirty-five, three years before Valadon's death, which means we meet her late in life, looking back. I like this kind of piece, a portrait of an artist built out of a single moment of reflection, much as a good novel can be. The magazine's headline says Valadon lives again thanks to Hiegel, which is high praise for an actress of her standing.

Down on the Riviera, the Musée des Beaux-Arts de Nice is offering guided visits of an exhibition called De la scène à la toile, from the stage to the canvas. The listing doesn't give dates, but the title alone points to a rich theme, how performance, its gestures, costumes and lighting, gets carried into paint. If you enjoy dance documentaries, as you do, you will know how much of that world has been seen through painters' eyes.

Then there is a lovely, small idea from Radio France. It asks listeners what music they can hear in Vilhelm Hammershøi's painting Paysage de Lejre. The text is brief, but the question is the thing. Hammershøi is a painter of hush, of muted greys and stillness, and a quiet Danish landscape does seem to hum with something just out of reach. It would make a good exercise, perhaps even for a class: put the picture on the screen, ask your pupils what they hear, and then have them write it down. You may find that the descriptions turn quickly into poetry.

Speaking of art and the written word, on BBC Radio 4's Front Row there is a forty-two-minute episode with the thriller writer Karin Slaughter. She talks about adapting her novel The Good Daughter for television, and the story is set in her native Georgia. Hearing a novelist explain what is kept, what is changed and what is lost when a book becomes a series is always instructive, and with thrillers in particular, where so much depends on pacing and withheld information, it is fascinating. The same episode also has a segment on an exhibition in Norwich about the kiss in art, so there is something for the picture lover too. It would suit a walk or a quiet evening.

Now to the lives behind the images. The National Gallery in London has published, today, a three-part film series called Linked Lives: Art and Empire. It looks at how the gallery's early history was shaped by empire and colonialism, and it draws on the research of Dr Sean Cham into the lives behind the paintings, including enslaved people who are so often left out of institutional history. This is the kind of work that makes you look at a familiar canvas differently, asking who is in the background, who paid for the frame, who is never named. Readers of historical fiction will recognise the instinct. Some of the best novels do precisely this, giving a voice to the people history left in the margin, and it is good to see a great gallery doing it in its own way.

In a similar spirit, Hyperallergic reviews a new documentary on the life of Romare Bearden, the collage artist. Piecing together a life is the reviewer's phrase, and it fits an artist who pieced together images. What I like in the review is that the best moments of the film, in the reviewer's view, are those in which we simply watch people engage with his work. That says something true about art films in general. The talking heads can be informative, but the real life of a picture is often in somebody's face as they look at it.

Finally, a handful of stories from The Guardian's art and design pages, mostly photographic.

The first is about Jill Posener, whose witty, feminist photographs of the nineteen eighties answered misogyny and Thatcherite conservatism. Among them is a graffitied billboard she photographed on London's Farringdon Road in nineteen seventy-nine. A retrospective now marks fifty years of her work. The article is carried by her own words, and one line stands out: she says she railed against the stereotype of the humourless lesbian. Her answer was humour, sharp and cheeky, and it sounds as though the pictures still raise a smile while making their point. There is a real lesson in that about tone, how a joke can be the most serious tool in the box.

The second is a gallery of photographs by Colin McPherson, from his project Catching the Tide, a portrait of Scotland's salmon fishers. The Guardian presents it as a moving record of a way of life that is disappearing. It is mostly about the images rather than the text, so it is something to look at rather than listen to, but I imagine the weather, the water and the weathered faces are the heart of it.

The third looks across the world. From now until the second of May, twenty twenty-seven, the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York is showing A Long Shadow, which brings together fifteen artists, with prints, books, magazines and a video installation, to show how Japanese photographers documented postwar Japan. The Guardian's gallery shows punks, sex workers and a society in transition. It is the first show of Japanese photography at the Met in more than thirty years, which makes it a significant moment, even if it is a long way from Les Adrets.

And one last item for the reading pile. The Guardian also reviews a new travelogue, With Wittgenstein in a Gay Sauna, which explores queer subcultures in Budapest, Prague and other central European cities and challenges the region's reputation for illiberalism. The headline quotes a striking claim, that homosexuality was coined by a Hungarian. The book touches on language, on Wittgenstein, and on an art exhibition about masculinity, so it is as much a book about words and ideas as about places. It sounds like the sort of travel writing that makes you rethink a map.

That is the morning's art news, Yamuna, and I hope something here sends you towards a gallery, a good book or a quiet moment with a Danish landscape and a pair of open ears.

literature.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a big couple of days for English-language fiction, with a surprising Booker Prize result at the centre, and plenty of good reading around it.

The news first. On the tenth of November, M. John Harrison won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything. He is eighty-one, which makes him the oldest winner in the prize's history. The Los Angeles Times has the fullest account of the announcement. Several outlets are also noting that he is the first science-fiction author to take the prize, and The Guardian words it a little more carefully, calling it the first win for a science-fiction-leaning novel.

The novel is apocalyptic and set on the Kent coast. In an interview with The Guardian, Harrison talks about hope and the state of the world, and he describes us as dream-walking into a desperate situation. That is the kind of line that makes you want to hear the whole conversation. The New Statesman has a lighter encounter with him, in which he admits he was, in his words, as nervous as a cat on the night. After a long career, that is rather endearing.

For a more reflective angle, The Conversation has an essay calling the book a wonder of weird fiction for our incomprehensible times. It reads the novel as writing that speaks to its moment, which is worth a look if strange narrators and unsettled atmospheres appeal. And The Guardian asks whether the win means a so-called snobby literary establishment has finally accepted science fiction. Kazuo Ishiguro and others weigh in, and it's a useful piece on how prizes have treated the fantastic. It might even make a good starting point for a class discussion about genre labels, and who decides what counts as literary.

Staying with inventive storytelling, The Guardian also reviews The Man With Many Names by Georgi Gospodinov. He is the Bulgarian writer who won the International Booker, and this new book is a collection of forty stories. The reviewer praises its playfulness and its meditations on storytelling itself, and describes its subversions as Borgesian. It sounds like a book of tales that are aware they are tales, and enjoy it.

The Guardian also reviews Public Access Afterworld, the first novel from Jane Schoenbrun. Its narrator is Bethany Peters, a trans content moderator at a YouTube-like company, whose job is to watch disturbing material all day. The reviewer calls it a wry and fun descent into the dark world behind our screens, with a strong narrator at its heart. If you like a thriller with a distinctive voice, this could be one to note down.

On a smaller scale, Literary Hub has published the opening of a short story called No Such Thing as Monday. Its narrator tracks down a sister she has never sought out, following bus routes to find where she works. It is only the beginning, but the voice is intriguing, and the premise of a quiet, almost detective-like pursuit is hard to resist.

Now to the past, and to how books and their authors are remembered. Literary Hub has an article about Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin. He has gone uncredited for three centuries, but recent archival discoveries are restoring his place in the story. It's literary history and a good tale at once, and a nice reminder that behind the most famous stories there are real people who were forgotten.

Also on Literary Hub, Adam Gopnik revisits Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises, which turns one hundred. He weighs its dated prejudices against its enduring hold on readers, and writes about the Lost Generation and about how a novel ages. It's a thoughtful essay, and the sort that could sit alongside a lesson on reading older texts with both admiration and a critical eye.

The Paris Review's Daily looks back at Barbara Trapido's debut novel, forty years after publication. The piece presents it as a book about how to live, how to love, and how to recover from heartbreak. It's a gentle retrospective, and it may send you to a writer whose emotional honesty has lasted.

Finally, two pieces about the craft and the wider world of reading. Tom Drury writes about working from America's so-called flyover country, drawing on a talk he gave at the Flyover Fictions conference in Innsbruck. It is an essay about place, and about what it means to write from somewhere people tend to pass over. And Literary Hub marks the hundredth Annotated Nightstand column, in which the translator Katrina Dodson talks about what she is reading now and what comes next. Her work on Brazilian literature gives the conversation real interest for anyone who loves language and translation.

So, a prize for a late-career writer, some playful tales, and a few forgotten stories brought back into the light; I hope something in there finds its way onto your nightstand.
literature.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a rich couple of days in the reading world, with a surprising Booker winner at the centre, and around him some lovely pieces on storytelling, old books and the way voices carry across time.

Let me begin with the big news. On the tenth of November, M. John Harrison won the 2026 Booker Prize for his novel The End of Everything. He is eighty-one, which makes him the oldest author ever to win the prize for fiction, and he is also being described as the first science-fiction writer to take it. The Los Angeles Times has the fullest account of the announcement, and several other outlets have carried the story, though some, like Lifestyle Asia in Hong Kong, give little more than the headline.

What interests me most is not the record, but the book and the man. The Guardian has an interview with Harrison under a title that rather stops you in your tracks: "We are dream-walking into a desperate situation." The End of Everything is an apocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast, and in the conversation he talks about the alien-invasion shape of the story as a kind of wake-up call. He also talks about hope, and about the state of the world. The Guardian presents him as someone who looks clearly at where we are without pretending to cheer us up. If you like narrators who see the world a little aslant, that is a good sign. A coastline in Kent is such an English, such a familiar setting, and the idea of setting the end of the world there has something wonderfully unsettling about it. The ordinary becomes the strange.

For a lighter side of the same man, the New Statesman also spoke to him. His line there is that he was "as nervous as a cat" on winning. I like that very much. After a long career, to be eighty-one and still nervous at a podium is oddly reassuring. It is a short, personable piece, and it suggests a writer with a dry sense of humour about the whole business of prizes.

Then there is the more thoughtful reading of the book itself. The Conversation has an essay calling The End of Everything "a wonder of weird fiction for our incomprehensible times." The phrase "weird fiction" is worth pausing on. It is a tradition of stories in which the strange is never fully explained, and in which the reader is left to sit with what cannot be understood. The essay argues that this suits our moment, when so much of the news feels hard to make sense of. For a teacher, it might be a good way into a conversation with older pupils about why a story that refuses to explain itself can feel more truthful than one that does.

And that leads neatly to the debate that has followed. The Guardian asks whether Harrison's win means that science fiction is finally accepted by what some call a "snobby" literary establishment. The piece reflects on the long-standing divide between genre and so-called literary fiction in publishing, and it gathers voices on the question, among them Kazuo Ishiguro. It is a useful read if you want to think about how prizes treat the fantastic. You might find, as I did, that the question is slightly older than the answers on offer. Many of the books you teach, I suspect, have always lived on both sides of that line. Think of how many novels on a school syllabus use the strange, the dystopian or the ghostly to say something true. The prize is perhaps less a conversion than a belated recognition of something readers have known for a long time.

There is one more report, from JournalArta, which calls the win a heartening late-career recognition. I agree with that spirit. For a writer at the end of a long working life to be seen so widely is a gift, and it sends readers back to the earlier work.

Let me turn now to two reviews in The Guardian, both of them about voices, and quite different from one another.

The first is of The Man With Many Names by Georgi Gospodinov, the International Booker winner. It is a collection of forty stories from Bulgaria. The reviewer calls it playful and profound, praising its inventiveness, its meditations on the nature of storytelling, and what they describe as Borgesian subversions. If you know Borges, you will recognise the pleasure being promised: stories that fold in on themselves, that treat the act of telling as the real subject, and that leave you slightly dizzy and delighted. Forty stories is also a generous number. It sounds like a book to dip into in the evening, one tale at a time, perhaps with a cup of tea after a long day of marking.

The second review is of Public Access Afterworld, the first novel by Jane Schoenbrun. It follows Bethany Peters, a trans content moderator at a company much like YouTube, whose job is to watch disturbing material so that the rest of us do not have to. The Guardian's reviewer calls it a wry, fun descent into the dark world behind our screens, with horror in the television static, and with a strong narrator at its centre. I like the contrast with Harrison. Here the end of the world is not on the horizon but in the glow of the monitor, and the voice leading us there is wry rather than weary. It may not be a book for the classroom, but if you enjoy a thriller with a distinctive narrator, it sounds worth a look.

Now to something older and, in its way, more romantic. Literary Hub has a fascinating article about Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin. For three centuries he has gone uncredited. The piece explains that recent archival discoveries are restoring his place in the story. I love this kind of literary detective work. We think of Aladdin as a tale that belongs to everyone and to no one, a story that simply floats in the air of childhood. To learn that behind it stands a real person, a traveller and storyteller who was written out of the record, is a reminder that stories have owners, and that history can be generous or careless about remembering them. It would make a charming small lesson on authorship, on who gets credited, and on how a tale travels from one language and culture to another.

Also from Literary Hub, and perhaps the piece I would most recommend to you personally, is Adam Gopnik's essay on The Sun Also Rises at one hundred. The Hemingway novel turns a century old, and Gopnik writes about it as an ode to the Lost Generation. He is honest about the dated prejudices in the book, and equally honest about why it still holds readers. That balance is exactly what a teacher needs: how to read a beloved book without excusing it, and without discarding it. The essay is about how a novel ages, and I suspect you will find phrases to borrow for your pupils. There is something moving about a book that is partly uncomfortable and still alive after a hundred years, and the question of what makes it survive is a very good one to put to a class.

Staying with books that have lasted, the Paris Review's Daily has a retrospective on Barbara Trapido's debut novel, forty years after it was published. The piece frames it as a book about how to live, how to love, and how to recover from heartbreak. That is a lovely way to describe a first novel, and it is a reminder that some of the most durable fiction is the kind that is quietly practical about the heart. If you do not know Trapido, this might be the nudge. It is the sort of novel that a reader tends to pass on to a friend with a note saying, you will like this.

Finally, a few pieces about craft and the reading life, all from Literary Hub.

There is the opening of a short story called No Such Thing as Monday. A narrator sets out to find a sister she has never sought out, following bus routes to the place where the sister works. I like the premise very much. The idea of finding a person by following public transport, one route and one stop at a time, is quietly suspenseful, and the narrative voice, according to the introduction, is intriguing. It is only the beginning of a story, so it is an easy thing to read in a few minutes and see whether it draws you in.

Then there is the hundredth Annotated Nightstand column, in which the translator Katrina Dodson talks about what she is reading now and what she will read next. Dodson works with Brazilian literature, so her reading list is likely to be full of language, of choices about how a sentence travels from one tongue to another. A hundredth column is a small milestone for the series, and it is a pleasant way to find new titles from someone who thinks about words for a living.

And last, Tom Drury writes about writing from America's "flyover country," drawing on a talk he gave at the Flyover Fictions conference in Innsbruck. It is an essay about place and the craft of writing: what it means to write from the places that travellers pass over rather than visit, and what the writer sees there. I find there is something delightful about that talk being given in Innsbruck, which is not so very far from your own mountains, a European audience listening to a novelist from the American middle. It is a good reminder that a place does not have to be famous to be rich in stories, which is a thought I suspect you share when you walk the paths above the Grésivaudan.

So, to gather it all together. The week's headline is a prize for a strange and apocalyptic book from an eighty-one-year-old who admits to feeling nervous as a cat. Around it sit stories about voices, from a content moderator in the static to a narrator following buses to find her sister, and some lovely reflections on books that have outlasted their moment, from Hemingway to Trapido to the almost-forgotten author behind Aladdin.

If you have time for only one piece today, I would choose the Gopnik essay, and if you have time for two, add the Guardian interview with Harrison. Enjoy your reading, Yamuna, and may your cup of tea stay warm while the pages turn.

around.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Here is what is stirring around you this Thursday, with a good deal of music and theatre on the way for the weekend, and a llama to finish.

Let me start in Chambéry, with an exhibition that I think will appeal to you. Unidivers reports on a show of Albanian portraits, called "icons", of faces that a dictatorship once tried to erase. The write-up is brief, so I can't tell you the dates or the venue, but the idea is striking: history told through faces, and through the simple stubbornness of images surviving. It's the sort of thing that sits well beside a novel about memory and censorship. Chambéry is also preparing its Christmas market. L'Essor Savoyard has a preview of what is new for the 2026 edition, though the details weren't given, so it's one to watch for as December approaches.

Now music, which is richest on Saturday the fourteenth of November. In Grenoble, Le Dauphiné Libéré announces an organ concert of Bach at the church of Saint-Joseph. I have no time or programme to give you, but Bach on a church organ is a lovely way to spend a November Saturday. The same day, in Corenc, there is a concert to raise money so that an assistance dog can be offered to victims. Again the details are sparse, but it is a kind cause and a close neighbour of Grenoble. And a little further ahead, on Thursday the nineteenth of November at the MC2 in Grenoble, the singer Raphaël will meet the public before his concert, in a session organised with Le Dauphiné Libéré. It's a chance to hear an artist talk about his work before he sings it.

On the stage side, several things open tomorrow, Friday the thirteenth. At half past seven in the evening, the Espace Culturel Paul Jargot in Crolles stages a performance called "Les enfants c'est moi". The listing gives no more than that, but it is the nearest evening of live performance to you. The same day, the Espace culturel Le Coléo in Pontcharra hosts an event called "Balle de Match". I'm afraid its nature is unclear from the listing, so you may want to look it up before setting out. In Grenoble, from the twelfth to the fifteenth of November, there is a show with the cheerfully blunt title "Les cons c'est les autres", and again there is no description to go on, so its tone is anyone's guess.

For something a little different, at five in the evening on Friday the thirteenth, the Saint Exupéry media library in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin offers a virtual reality experience called "Insider-outsider". Details are scarce, but a title like that suggests something about belonging and exclusion, and it would be interesting to see how a story is told when you step inside it.

If you're thinking about a longer run of theatre, Grenoble Mag reports that the Festival international de théâtre action is back, with eight socially engaged new productions, running until the twenty-fifth of November. The pieces themselves aren't described, but the focus is clearly serious, and there's time to catch something over the next two weeks.

If you'd rather simply browse for ideas, two round-ups may help. The website jds.fr has nine suggestions for Grenoble over the weekend of the thirteenth to the fifteenth of November. It mentions a ballet, a much-anticipated indie rock concert, and mini-golf in the style of Alcatraz, which sounds delightfully eccentric. And ici.fr has a wider list of outings across Isère for the tenth to the sixteenth of November, though I only have the headline.

Finally, some gentler local stories. Grenoble Mag tells us the twenty-ninth Festival des solidarités has begun, opening a month of events devoted to solidarity. I don't have the programme, but it runs through the coming weeks. Ici-Grenoble.org reports that an orchard is being planted at the self-managed university in Grenoble. It's a short item, but a pleasing one: fruit trees going into the ground, with the harvest still years away.

And my favourite of the lot comes from France 3 Alpes. At a sheep farm in Poisat, near Grenoble, two shepherds have chosen to protect their flock from wolves not with a traditional patou dog but with a llama called Jeff. They say the flock is now calm and settled. It's a small, charming tale of animals looking after one another, and rather like a fable in the making.

That's your morning, Yamuna: may your weekend have a little Bach in it, and perhaps a llama's calm.
