And a little further ahead, on Thursday the nineteenth of November, the MC2 in Grenoble is holding a chance to meet the singer Raphaël before his concert. It's organised with Le Dauphiné Libéré, and it's an opportunity to hear an artist talk about his work before he goes on stage.

Now to the theatre and live performance, where there's quite a lot going on, though the listings are brief. Tomorrow, Friday the thirteenth, at half past seven in the evening, the Espace Culturel Paul Jargot in Crolles stages a performance called Les enfants c'est moi. Crolles is close to home for you, and the listing gives no further detail, so you'd be going on the strength of the title alone. Sometimes that's the best way to go to the theatre. The same day, the Espace culturel Le Coléo in Pontcharra hosts an event called Balle de Match, listed as arts and culture. I'm afraid the listing doesn't say what form it takes, so I can't tell you whether it's theatre, music or something else entirely. In Grenoble, a show with the rather bracing title Les cons c'est les autres runs from today, the twelfth, until Sunday the fifteenth. Isère Attractivité lists it as a cultural show, and that's all it says about it.

There's also something more substantial for theatre lovers. Grenoble Mag reports that the Festival international de théâtre action is back, with eight socially engaged new productions, running until the twenty-fifth of November. The article gives little detail on the individual pieces, but the focus is clear: theatre that has something to say about the world around it, and that's a fortnight of possibilities rather than a single date to hit.

For a wider look at the weekend, jds.fr has put together nine ideas for Grenoble from Friday the thirteenth to Sunday the fifteenth. The list includes a ballet, a much-anticipated indie rock concert, and, I rather like this one, mini-golf in the style of Alcatraz. I don't have the name of the ballet or the company, but since you enjoy dance, it may be worth looking at the full article to see what's on offer. For something broader across the département, ici.fr has a roundup of outing ideas across Isère for the tenth to the sixteenth of November. Again, only the headline came through, but it's there if you'd like more choice.

Now to something a little different. At the Médiathèque Saint Exupéry in Montbonnot-Saint-Martin, tomorrow, Friday the thirteenth, at five in the afternoon, there's a virtual reality experience called Insider-outsider. The listing doesn't describe what you'll see, but the title alone suggests something about belonging and exclusion. It's an unusual thing to find in a village media library, and it might be an interesting counterpoint to the more traditional evenings I've mentioned.

If you're drawn to history and memory, there's an exhibition in Chambéry that I think could be the most interesting item today. Unidivers reports on a show of Albanian portraits, described as icons, the faces that a dictatorship tried to erase. The text I have is short, so I can't tell you the dates, the venue or the artists. But the idea is striking: portraits as an act of memory, a way of putting back on the wall what a regime tried to remove. It's the sort of history that comes through faces rather than essays, and I suspect it would resonate with the way you like novels to teach the past. It might make a good bridge with a class too, if you ever wanted to talk about how images are censored and how they survive.

Then there are the gentler, more rural and community stories. France 3 Alpes reports from a sheep farm in Poisat, near Grenoble, where two shepherds have decided to protect their flock from wolves in an unusual way. Instead of the traditional patou dog, they've brought in a llama called Jeff. They say the flock is now calm and settled, and that the llama keeps watch. It's a charming story of animals working together, and Jeff deserves a place in any pastoral tale. In Grenoble itself, Ici-Grenoble.org reports that an orchard is being planted at the Université autogérée, the self-managed university. The report is very short, but there's something hopeful in the image of fruit trees going into the ground, trees whose reward comes years later, and which are planted by people who expect to still be around, or at least to leave something behind.

And a more civic note. Grenoble Mag tells us that the twenty-ninth Festival des solidarités is under way, opening a month of events devoted to solidarity. The article doesn't give a programme, but a month-long festival suggests plenty of choice, and it's worth looking out for events near you as they're announced.

Finally, a little further ahead, since it's nearly that time of year. L'Essor Savoyard has a preview of what's new at the Chambéry Christmas market for 2026. The headline promises novelties, but I don't have the dates or the details. It's one to keep in mind for December, perhaps for a stroll and a hot drink.

So, to gather it all together: if you want a quiet, beautiful evening, Bach in Grenoble on Saturday is the one. If you'd prefer to be surprised, Crolles tomorrow evening or the festival of theatre action will do the job. And if you have a free afternoon and a taste for history told through faces, Chambéry's Albanian icons look well worth the trip.

Have a lovely day, Yamuna, and may your weekend be full of good music and, with luck, a llama or two.

bfi.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a quiet two days for official BFI news, but plenty of material has turned up around the edges of the programme, and some of it is lovely.

Let me begin with Armistice Day, because The Washington Post published a piece on John McCrae's "In Flanders Fields", tracing how a patriotic poem came to be heard as an anti-war anthem. It's really about how a text's meaning shifts over time and with its readers. That's a useful idea for any class on war poetry, and for first-years who assume a poem means one fixed thing.

Hamlet, from session twenty twenty-seven, is well represented. The strongest item is from the BBC, an inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while he was dying of Aids. The headline quotes someone calling it "a hell of a thing to take on", and the piece is about how a role can take on enormous personal weight. It could move a class from Hamlet's own mortality to the question of what an actor brings to the part. Alongside it, ATV Today reports that the company Hail to the Thief has released new production photographs of its Hamlet. It's brief, but photographs are a handy prompt for staging discussion: what do you see, and what choices were made? And since you love dance, River 949 covers Queensland Ballet's Hamlet, a dance adaptation of the play. The text I have is only a headline, so I can't say more, but it does raise a nice question for students: what is left of Hamlet when the words are taken away?

Staying with the twenty twenty-seven list, Blake gets two outings from Britannica. One looks at how "The Lamb" and "The Tyger" work as contrasting symbols, which is a clear, classroom-ready way into the innocence and experience pairing, and suits seconde or première. The other asks how the death of Blake's brother Robert affected his art and poetry. It's a useful piece of background for teaching Songs of Innocence and of Experience, and I'd pair the two: one for the poems, one for the life behind them.

Two other plays from that session are on stages this week. Florida Weekly has a piece headed "All's fair in love and deception" about The Rivals. The text is short, so it's probably a review or feature, but it's a reminder that Sheridan's comedy is still being staged. And in Kilcullen, in Ireland, the Kilcullen Diary announces that tickets are now on sale for a production of Brian Friel's Dancing at Lughnasa. There's little detail beyond that, but it's good to see it being performed.

Now to the oral themes. The Boar, a student paper, asks why we are so obsessed with dystopia, with that odd mix of triumph and hopelessness. It's a natural prompt for The Handmaid's Tale, 1984 or The Road, and as a student voice it may be easy for pupils to answer back to. On the same territory, OutNow has an interview with Raoul Peck about his documentary Orwell: 2+2=5, touching on political art and the power of knowledge. It connects to 1984, though the political framing is worth weighing before you bring it into class, and I'd treat it as one angle rather than a neutral one.

On a warmer note, the Alameda Post reports that Alameda High School has staged what it calls a delightful Emma. A student production of Jane Austen is heartening, and a good example for your pupils of young people taking on a classic.

For Atonement, IndulgExpress looks at how Keira Knightley's green gown in the film was designed to symbolise envy and longing. It's about costume, not the book, but it links neatly to McEwan's imagery, and you could ask students where the novel does the same work in words alone. And The Times of India has a piece on Maya Angelou renting hotel rooms simply to write. It offers author context for I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, and the detail is a good hook for a first lesson: where and how does a writer find the space to tell the truth?

Two last items are about reading itself. The Irish Independent interviews the novelist Yiyun Li, who says she reads War and Peace and Moby-Dick every year, and has done so for nearly twenty years. It's a lovely reflection on rereading, and it may speak to you as a teacher as much as to your students. And finally, Britannica poses the question of how Bleak House criticises the legal system. Only the question is given, and the novel isn't one of the programme works, but it's the sort of book that teaches law and social history better than a textbook, which I know you value.

So, plenty to dip into over a coffee, and perhaps a few ideas to carry into the classroom.
bfi.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle day in the BFI corner, with plenty for session twenty twenty-seven, a few oral-theme gems, and one or two pieces that might simply be good company over coffee.

Let me begin with Hamlet, which turns up three times and in three quite different guises.

The one I'd put first is a BBC piece, billed as the inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while he was dying of Aids. The headline quotes someone calling it "a hell of a thing to take on", and that phrase is worth pausing on. What the piece offers a teacher is a very human way into the play. Hamlet is a character who spends five acts thinking about death, mortality and what is left behind, and here is an actor who carried those questions on stage in the most personal way imaginable. I'd be careful with it in class, because it is a sombre story and you will know best how your première group would receive it. But for a lesson on how a role can take on weight beyond the text, or how performance changes what lines mean, it looks like a rich piece of context. It might suit a teacher's own preparation even if it never reaches the students.

The second Hamlet item is much lighter. A company called Hail to the Thief has released new production photography for its Hamlet, reported by ATV Today. It's brief, and I only have the fact of the photographs, not what they show. Still, production stills are a handy resource. You could put two or three images on the board and ask students what the staging seems to be saying about Elsinore, about the ghost, or about Hamlet himself, before they have read a word of commentary. It's a low-effort, high-yield way into a discussion of directorial choices.

The third, and I suspect the one you'll enjoy most, comes from River 949, which covers Queensland Ballet's production of Hamlet. This is a dance adaptation of Shakespeare's play. All I have is the headline, so I can't tell you about choreography or casting. But it joins two of your loves, and it raises a lovely question for students: what happens to a play built almost entirely from language when you take the words away? How do you dance soliloquy, or madness, or a ghost? Even without seeing the production, that question could make a good short discussion or a creative task, perhaps asking students to describe, in prose, how they would stage "To be or not to be" with no speech at all.

Now to poetry, and the way a poem's meaning can shift under our feet. The Washington Post published a piece on Armistice Day tracing how John McCrae's "In Flanders Fields" went from being a patriotic poem to something read as an anti-war anthem. That is a wonderful subject for a classroom. The poem is short, memorable and strongly shaped, and the idea that the same words can be heard so differently depending on who is reading and when is exactly the kind of thing première students can grasp and argue about. It links war poetry, history and reception in a single text. If you teach The Return of the Soldier next year, the piece could also serve as a gentle opening onto how the First World War is remembered, though that would be my suggestion rather than anything in the article. A simple exercise would be to read the poem aloud twice, once as a recruitment piece and once as a protest, and see how much the voice has to change.

Staying with poetry, there are two Britannica pieces on William Blake, who is of course on the session twenty twenty-seven list with Songs of Innocence and of Experience. The first asks how "The Lamb" and "The Tyger" work as contrasting symbols in his poetry. It looks like a clear, classroom-ready angle on the pairing of innocence and experience, and I'd say it suits seconde or première well. These two poems are almost a ready-made lesson, a gentle creature and a fearsome one, each prompting questions about who made it. Britannica is a reference source rather than a critical essay, so I'd treat it as a clean starting point rather than the last word.

The second Blake piece asks how the death of his brother Robert affected his art and poetry. I only have the question, not the answer, so I can't tell you what Britannica concludes. But it is a useful reminder that biography can be a way in for students who find Blake forbidding. Grief, loss and the loss of innocence sit rather close together, and a short biographical note can make the Songs feel less like a puzzle and more like writing by someone who had known real sorrow. I would offer it as background and let the poems do the heavy lifting.

On to the stage. Two session twenty twenty-seven plays are in the news, both rather modestly.

Florida Weekly has a piece headlined "All's fair in love and deception in The Rivals". It's brief, and I'd guess a review or feature on a production of Sheridan's comedy. I can't tell you more than that. But the headline itself catches something useful for students: The Rivals is a play of disguises, false names and romantic misunderstanding, and deception is a good thread to pull on. You could ask a seconde class to list every lie or pretence in the first act and decide which ones are harmless. It is also a pleasing reminder that this eighteenth-century comedy is still being staged far from where it began.

Then there is a small local announcement from the Kilcullen Diary: ticket sales have opened for a production of Brian Friel's Dancing at Lughnasa in Kilcullen. There is very little detail beyond that. But for a play so bound up with music, memory and the dance that breaks out in the kitchen, it's a nice sign of a community taking it on. If any of your students are curious about how the play lives outside the classroom, a notice like this is a good prompt: amateur and local productions are often where plays like this are kept alive.

Staying with young people and the stage, the Alameda Post reports that Alameda High School has put on what it calls a delightful Emma. Emma is on your oral themes list, and I found this cheering in itself: teenagers taking on Austen, a writer whose irony and social comedy can seem remote, and apparently making something enjoyable of it. It's a good-news item, and it might be worth mentioning to students who think a classic has to be a chore. You could even ask them what they would cut or change to put Emma on a school stage, which is quite a sharp way of making them decide what matters most in the novel.

Now to the oral themes more broadly, starting with dystopia. The Boar, a student newspaper, has a piece asking why we are so obsessed with dystopian fiction, with its odd mixture of triumph and hopelessness. That mixture is a rather good description of how many of your oral texts feel. The Handmaid's Tale, 1984 and The Road all hold out the possibility of resistance or survival while refusing easy comfort. It's a student piece, so I would read it as a fresh, youthful voice rather than a scholarly authority. For that reason it might actually be useful to pass to students: it shows someone not so far from their own age asking a good question about fiction. You could ask them whether the pleasure of dystopia is fear, warning or something stranger.

Related, though I'd handle it with a light touch, is an interview in OutNow with Raoul Peck about his documentary Orwell: 2+2=5, discussing political art and the power of knowledge. It connects directly to 1984. The interview's political framing is worth weighing, and I know you prefer to steer clear of polemic. So I'd read it for what it says about how Orwell's ideas travel into film and what art can do with knowledge and truth, rather than for any political line. If you do use anything from it, perhaps keep it to the question of why the equation two plus two equals five still carries such force as an image.

Two items offer author or image context for oral texts. The first is from The Times of India, about Maya Angelou's habit of renting hotel rooms simply in order to write. The piece is about the unusual routine she followed to concentrate. For I Know Why the Caged Bird Sings, that's a lovely classroom hook. Students tend to be fascinated by how writers actually work, and the idea of a hotel room as a place to think is vivid and slightly surprising. It humanises the author before the class meets the book, and it might prompt them to talk about where and how they concentrate best.

The second is a piece from IndulgExpress about how Keira Knightley's green gown in the film of Atonement was designed to symbolise envy and longing. This is film-world material, and I know that's low on your list, so I'll keep it brief. But the angle is really about symbolism, and symbolism is something students can test against the novel. McEwan's text is full of imagery of its own. You could ask them to think about what a visual symbol can do that a sentence cannot, and the reverse, and whether the green of that dress feels earned by the book. That could make a neat comparative exercise for a class that has seen the film.

Finally, two items about reading itself. The Irish Independent interviews the Chinese-born American novelist Yiyun Li, who says she reads War and Peace and Moby-Dick every year, and has done so for nearly twenty years. I only have that line, but it's a fine one. It speaks to rereading as a practice, the idea that a great book is not finished once you have reached the last page, and that you change while the book stays put. For a literature teacher it is a quiet, encouraging thought. It might even be worth sharing with students, especially those preparing a text they have to live with for a full year.

And last, Britannica asks how Bleak House criticises the legal system. I only have the question, not the answer. Bleak House is not on the programme, though Dickens is there through Great Expectations. Still, I know you value novels that teach history and society better than any essay could, and Bleak House is a good example, with its portrait of law as a slow, devouring machine. If you wanted a short side-route for students who like Dickens, this might be a way to show how a novel can make an institution feel like a character.

So that's the corner for today: Hamlet in three forms, Blake in two, a pair of plays on local stages, a few oral-theme hooks, and a rereading novelist to keep you company. Have a lovely day up in Les Adrets.

france.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Thursday the twelfth of November, and the news from France is shaped by yesterday's Armistice Day, with a storm coming in from the south and a few good things to read and watch.

Let me begin with remembrance, since it offers some lovely material for a literature teacher. Franceinfo has published a reconstruction of the last days and hours before the armistice was signed at Compiègne, in Marshal Foch's railway carriage. It draws on the writings of Captain Paul Laperche, the interpreter who was in the room, so you get the history through a firsthand witness rather than a textbook voice. Franceinfo also visited the Collège du Vieux Chêne in Chessy, in Seine-et-Marne, where pupils marked the day with readings from soldiers' letters and a song. They spoke for themselves for the first time, and one of them said it was more interesting than a lesson, which I suspect you'll enjoy hearing. In Paris, Emmanuel Macron paid tribute to Georges Clemenceau and the Unknown Soldier. It was his last Armistice ceremony as head of state, and this year's emphasis fell on Marshal Foch.

On a lighter note, The Local France has two small language items that fit the day. The word of the day is bleuet, the cornflower, which the piece links to one of two French flowers associated with public holidays. And the expression of the day is "Tu parles !", which doesn't mean "you're talking", of course, but is a retort signalling scepticism or irony. It's a handy one for any class working on the gap between what is said and what is meant.

Now for culture. The Guardian has dug out an archive piece from the eleventh of November, 1976, about five British chefs cooking a lunch at Maxim's in Paris, set against the long-running rivalry between British and French cooking. It's described as witty and richly written, and it offers a window onto a vanished dining world, so it may be worth a few minutes with a cup of tea. The Guardian also reviews Whispers in the Woods, Vincent Munier's French nature documentary, filmed in the Vosges. It follows a father and son in search of lynx, foxes and deer, and the reviewer calls it a tender study of human and animal interaction, with paddling in the moonlight. It's quiet, emotionally driven and visually stylised, quite unlike the Attenborough approach. A gentle, atmospheric watch, by the sound of it.

Now the weather, which matters today. Storm Charles has already left Portugal with heavy rain, and residents there were urged to stay indoors. It is now reaching southern France, and the advice is to be vigilant. On the Côte d'Azur, franceinfo reports heavy rain causing traffic jams, a road accident, landslides and other disruption. That's not close to Grenoble, but if you have friends or travel plans towards the coast, it's worth a quick check before anyone sets off.

Closer to home in spirit, there are two stories about life away from the big cities. The government plans to raise the number of so-called medical buses to one hundred by the end of 2027, with seventy new ones, to serve rural areas that are short of doctors. And on Tuesday, an official report called for stronger cooperation between France and Switzerland on water management around Geneva, the Ain and Haute-Savoie. Its argument, which is nicely put, is that floods and droughts do not care about human borders. With the Alps on your doorstep, you'll see why it matters.

In schools, there's a news item from Chelles, near Paris, where an elected official was attacked outside a lycée. Emmanuel Macron has voiced his support for her. I mention it simply because it concerns a school, and you may hear about it in the staff room.

For something to lift the spirits, the European Space Agency has published its first large release of images and data from the Euclid telescope, which was launched in 2023. The pictures show hundreds of millions of galaxies. It's good news that belongs to everyone, not just France, and it's the sort of thing that makes a classroom go quiet for a moment.

And finally, La Mire's daily video for the twelfth of November is out. It's a quick, light zapping through French television, and this edition covers the Armistice commemoration, an anniversary segment, and a history teacher in the Aisne. Some segments touch on politics, so you can skip those, but the teacher in the Aisne might be a pleasant few minutes for you.

That's the roundup for today, Yamuna. Keep an umbrella handy and a good book closer still.
france.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It's Thursday the twelfth of November, and the French news of the past two days has been shaped largely by Armistice Day, with a storm, a few small cultural pleasures and a rather lovely piece of space news alongside it.

Let me begin with the eleventh of November, because several stories gather around it. Franceinfo has published a reconstruction of the last days and hours before the armistice was signed at Compiègne, in Marshal Foch's railway carriage. What makes it special is its source. It draws on the writings of Captain Paul Laperche, the interpreter who was in the carriage. So instead of a distant summary, you get a witness at the table, someone whose job was to carry words from one language to another at one of the most consequential moments of the century. For a teacher of literature, that is rather irresistible: a narrator with a precise vantage point, noticing the small details of a room where history turned. It might even make a good short reading for a class, a firsthand voice used to open up the question of how we know what we know about the past.

In the same spirit, franceinfo visited the Collège du Vieux Chêne in Chessy, in Seine-et-Marne, where pupils marked the day by reading out soldiers' letters and singing a song. One of the striking things about the report is that the pupils spoke for themselves for the first time at this commemoration, rather than standing quietly in the background. One of them says it's more interesting than during a lesson, which I suspect you will take in the good humour in which it was meant. There is something moving in teenagers lending their voices to letters written by young men not much older than themselves, and it is a good reminder that a letter read aloud can do what a textbook paragraph often can't.

On the official side, Emmanuel Macron paid tribute to Georges Clemenceau and to the Unknown Soldier at the national ceremony. Franceinfo notes that this is his last Armistice ceremony as head of state, and that this year the emphasis was placed on Marshal Foch. It was a solemn occasion, as you would expect, about memory and the First World War rather than anything else.

If you want something lighter on the same theme, The Local France has chosen as its French word of the day the bleuet, the cornflower. The piece links it to one of two French flowers associated with public holidays, and it fits the eleventh of November neatly. It is a small, pretty piece of vocabulary, and the kind of word that carries a whole season of remembrance inside it. Do keep it in your pocket if the subject comes up with your classes.

And while we are speaking of days that have just passed, franceinfo also ran a practical guide to what was open and shut on Wednesday. Most hypermarkets were open, while most banks, hairdressers and estate agencies were closed. It is a little late to be useful for this year, but it is a handy thing to remember for next time you are planning a bank-holiday errand in Grenoble or down in the valley from Les Adrets.

La Mire, the daily television zapping you like to keep an eye on, has its edition for today, the twelfth of November. It picks up the Armistice commemoration, includes an anniversary segment on Verdun, and spends a few minutes with a history teacher in the Aisne. It is quick and light, and the history teacher is probably the part you will enjoy most. A few of the segments touch on politics, so you can skip those without missing anything.

Now for something with a literary flavour of its own. The Guardian has republished, from its archive, a piece dated the eleventh of November nineteen seventy-six, about British and French culinary rivalry. Five British chefs cooked a lunch at Maxim's in Paris, a rather bold thing to do, given the setting and the long history of friendly sparring between the two kitchens. The piece is admired for its witty, richly written prose, and also for the window it opens onto a vanished world of dining. Archive journalism like this can be a pleasure in itself, a little time capsule of tone and manners, and it would make an amusing example of period voice if you were ever looking for one.

Also from The Guardian, there is a review of Whispers in the Woods, a French nature documentary by Vincent Munier, filmed in the Vosges. It follows a father and son as they search for lynx, foxes and deer. The reviewer describes it as a tender study of human and animal interaction, and the title of the review mentions paddling in the moonlight, which tells you something about the mood. It is quiet, emotionally driven and visually stylised, and quite different from the Attenborough tradition of natural history. If you are in the mood for a gentle, atmospheric evening, it sounds like one for a winter night in the mountains, with the lights low.

And for the idiom corner, The Local France explains the expression "tu parles !". Despite the literal meaning, which is just "you speak", it is a retort that signals scepticism or irony, rather than stating the obvious. Think of it as the French way of saying "yeah, right" or "you must be joking", depending on the tone. For a teacher of English who works across both languages, it is a nice example of how tone does the work that dictionary meaning cannot, and it might even make a good prompt for a discussion with your pupils about irony and how it travels between languages.

Turning to the weather, which is the practical matter of the day. Storm Charles, which has already hit Portugal with heavy rain and led the authorities there to urge residents to stay indoors, is expected to reach southern France today, Thursday the twelfth. Franceinfo carries a warning that people will need to stay vigilant, and that is really the key message. Later in the day, the same outlet reported on the effects along the Côte d'Azur, where heavy rain has caused traffic jams, a road accident, landslides and other disruption. That is not especially close to Grenoble, but if you have friends or plans down on the coast, it is worth a quick check before anyone sets off, and it is a good moment to keep an eye on the forecast for your own area too.

A report with a rather closer connection to the Alps came out on Tuesday. An official report called for stronger cooperation between France and Switzerland on water management, around Geneva, the Ain and Haute-Savoie. Its central argument is neatly put: floods and droughts, it says, don't care about human borders. It is an interesting reminder that the rivers and rain which shape our landscape pay no attention to the lines on the map, and that managing them well means neighbours working together. The Local France has the story.

In matters of everyday life, The Local France also reports that the government plans to increase the number of so-called medical buses to one hundred by the end of twenty twenty-seven. That means seventy new ones, and they are meant to serve rural areas where doctors are scarce. It is a practical, rather hopeful idea, bringing care directly to places that have found it hard to keep it. For someone who loves the markets and villages of the countryside, it is the sort of story that shows how life beyond the cities is being thought about.

A word on schools, though it is a sombre one. HugoDécrypte reports that Emmanuel Macron has expressed his support for an elected official who was attacked outside a lycée in Chelles, near Paris. I mention it only because it concerns a school and violence against a public figure, and as a lycée teacher you may well want to know about it. There is nothing further in the report that I can add, so I will leave it there.

And finally, to end on a note of real wonder. The European Space Agency has published its first large release of images and data from the Euclid telescope, which was launched in twenty twenty-three. The pictures show hundreds of millions of galaxies. It is hard to take in a number like that, and perhaps that is the point: the sky is much fuller than we can easily imagine, and a telescope orbiting far from us has now brought some of it into view. It is good news from well beyond France, and the sort of thing that might send you looking up on a clear evening above the Grésivaudan, once the storm has passed.

That is the news for today, Yamuna, and I hope the weather is kind to you and your cornflowers.

good.short:
Good morning, Yamuna. Today's good news has a bookish streak, with a few late honours, some very old secrets coming to light, and a good deal of green returning to the world.

Let me begin with the literary headline. M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize for The End of Everything, and at eighty-one he becomes the oldest winner in the prize's history. Lifestyle Asia reports that he is also the first science-fiction author to take the honour, which feels like a quiet door opening. The novel is an apocalyptic story set on the Kent coast. In an interview with The Guardian, Harrison talks about hope and the state of the world, and the headline quotes him saying we are dream-walking into a desperate situation. He describes the book as a kind of alien-invasion wake-up call. The New Statesman has a lighter conversation with him, in which he admits he was as nervous as a cat on the night. And The Conversation calls the novel a wonder of weird fiction for our incomprehensible times, which is the sort of description that makes one want to open page one. After a long career, it is lovely to see a writer recognised like this.

Staying with stories, there is a good run of tales about history hiding in plain sight. Literary Hub has a piece on Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin. He has gone uncredited for some three hundred years, but recent archival discoveries are now restoring him to the story. It is a nice reminder that even our best-loved tales have authors, or at least sources, waiting to be remembered.

In Spain, researchers have found two hundred and eighty Ice Age engravings in a cave on the Mediterranean coast, the third-largest collection of its kind found there. Visitors had been walking past them for more than sixty years. Good News Network tells it well, and I rather like the thought of all those people passing by, with the drawings just out of sight.

Upworthy, meanwhile, has two discovery stories with a lot of charm. In the first, an archaeology PhD student reportedly found a lost Maya city while searching Google, on page sixteen of the results, which is further than most of us ever scroll. In the second, a man went looking for a friend's lost hammer and instead found more than fifteen thousand Roman coins. The piece suggests that the hunt mattered as history too, not just as luck.

Upworthy also offers something for the painters among your interests. Salvador Dalí had a habit of napping while holding a key, so that it would fall, clatter, and wake him with an idea still fresh from the edge of sleep. Scientists now think he may have been onto something, and that this half-asleep moment may really help creativity. It is a sweet link between surrealism and sleep research, and it might make a fun anecdote for a class on writing and imagination.

Now to the natural world, which has been busy. In Chile, the Atacama, often called the driest desert in the world, has burst into an exceptional bloom. Good News Network says some two hundred species are flowering, a few in places that had not bloomed since before the millennium. The seeds and tubers have been waiting underground all that time, patient as anything, and now the desert is in flower.

Also from Good News Network, there is a real conservation success in northern Spain. The Cantabrian brown bear population has roughly doubled over the last twenty years, from as few as a hundred and forty animals to about three hundred and seventy. The bears now range over a much wider area too, so this is an outcome, not just a hope.

And for something more imaginative, Reasons to be Cheerful, together with the Outrider Foundation, looks at the mossy cities of the future. The piece begins with Philip Wallisfurth, who in two thousand and twelve proposed using moss to save a hundred-and-fifty-year-old tree in Aachen. From there it imagines greener, softer cities. It is an inventive idea, and the sort of image a poet might enjoy.

Finally, two stories of people giving something back. Bonnie Fay is eighty-four and a piano player. Good News Network tells how she has returned to Bryn Mawr Village, the Pennsylvania nursing home where she was once a patient after Guillain-Barré syndrome, to give music to the residents. She had been paralysed, and now she plays for others, which is a recovery story that ends in generosity.

And The Optimist Daily, in its Local Changemakers series for twenty twenty-six, profiles Prince Bashangezi. He was an A-Level student at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe when COVID lockdowns cost him his schooling. He turned that loss into peer tutoring, helping other refugee students keep learning. As a teacher, you may find that one particularly moving.

That is the good news for today, and I hope it follows you gently through your morning, perhaps with a key in one hand and a good book in the other.
good.long:
Good morning, Yamuna. It has been a rich couple of days for good news, with a prize that rewards a very long writing life, some old secrets coming out of the ground, and a few quiet acts of kindness to finish on.

Let me begin with books, since I suspect that is where you would like to begin. The big story is the Booker Prize. M. John Harrison has won the twenty twenty-six prize for his novel The End of Everything, and he has made history twice over. At eighty-one, he is the oldest author ever to win it, and he is the first science-fiction author to take the honour. Lifestyle Asia in Hong Kong and the outlet JournalArta both carry the news, and it is a heartening thing, a late-career recognition for a writer many readers have perhaps still to discover.

Several outlets have gone deeper, and the coverage is worth a moment because the voices in it are so distinct. The Guardian has an interview in which Harrison talks about the book, an apocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast, and about his outlook on hope and the state of the world. The headline quotes him saying that we are dream-walking into a desperate situation, which is a striking phrase from someone who has just been handed one of literature's great prizes. The Guardian describes the book as a sort of alien invasion wake-up call. I would not want to say more about the plot than that, since the pieces I have only give us that outline. But a coastal English setting and an end-of-the-world mood is a fascinating combination, and I can imagine it having a quiet, unsettling music.

The New Statesman has a lighter conversation with him, and its headline is a lovely one: I was as nervous as a cat. There is something very human in that. Here is a man with decades of work behind him, now the oldest winner in the prize's history, and he admits to being a bundle of nerves on the night. If you ever want to show your première students that even celebrated writers are anxious people, that line might do it.

And then The Conversation has an essay calling the book a wonder of weird fiction for our incomprehensible times. I like that framing. It treats the novel as writing that speaks to its moment, the way strange fiction often does, by making the unfamiliar feel more honest than the familiar. For a teacher who loves unusual narrators and the way a story can reflect a period of history, it sounds like a good read to bookmark, whether or not the novel itself ends up on a syllabus.

Staying with stories, there is a fine piece in Literary Hub about Hanna Diab, an eighteenth-century Syrian adventurer whose life is thought to have inspired Aladdin. For some three centuries he has gone uncredited, which is a remarkable thing to say about the origin of one of the most famous tales in the world. The article describes how recent archival discoveries are now restoring his place in the story. I find this irresistible: literary history, an adventurer, and the quiet satisfaction of a name being returned to where it belongs. It is the kind of thing that reminds us that stories have authors and journeys, even when the world forgets them.

Now a little bridge between painting and ideas. Upworthy has a piece on Salvador Dalí and his peculiar nap trick. As the story goes, he would doze in a chair holding a key, and when he fell asleep the key would drop and the noise would wake him, hopefully with an idea fresh in his mind. What makes it good news is that scientists now think he may have been onto something. It is a pleasing link between art, creativity and sleep research, the notion that the drowsy edge of waking is a fertile place for imagination. If you are ever setting a creative-writing task with your classes, there is a rather charming experiment to be had there, though I will leave the choice of key to you.

From the arts, let us move to the ground itself, because this week has been generous with discoveries from the past. The first comes from Spain, and Good News Network reports it. Researchers have found two hundred and eighty Ice Age engravings in a cave on Spain's Mediterranean coast. It is the third-largest collection of such engravings found there. What makes it so extraordinary is that visitors had been walking past them for more than sixty years without seeing them. Prehistoric art, hidden in plain sight. I find that wonderfully humbling. Those lines were there the whole time, waiting for someone to look at the wall in just the right way, and to notice what generations of people had missed. It is a nice reminder, too, of how much of the human story is still to be read.

The second is one that I think you will enjoy for its sheer charm. Upworthy reports that a PhD student in archaeology accidentally found a lost Maya city while searching on Google. The detail that makes it memorable is that it was reportedly on page sixteen of the search results. Almost nobody looks at page sixteen. It is a lovely story about curiosity and patience, and about how discovery can come from persistence in an unfashionable corner. I cannot tell you more than that from what I have in front of me, but the image of a student scrolling patiently far past where most of us would give up is a good one.

And the third is a story that Upworthy tells under a rather wonderful headline: a man went looking for a lost hammer and found over fifteen thousand Roman coins instead. It began, the piece says, as a favour for a friend. The text is brief, so I cannot offer much more detail, but the shape of it is delightful, a modest errand turning into a significant archaeological find. The piece also suggests that the search itself mattered as history. Fifteen thousand coins is a number that is hard to picture, and one imagines that every one of them passed through someone's hands two thousand years ago.

Taken together, these three stories feel like a little lesson in how the past hides: under a cave wall, in a search engine, in the soil where you were looking for something else entirely.

Let me turn now to the natural world, where the news has been genuinely spectacular. In Chile, the Atacama Desert has burst into an exceptional bloom, according to Good News Network. This is a place recently described as the driest on Earth, and yet some two hundred species are now flowering. A few of them are blooming in places where nothing has been seen in flower since before the millennium. The explanation is the part I love best: seeds and tubers have been waiting underground, sometimes for years, ready to burst into life when conditions allow. There is a metaphor in that for patience that I will leave you to find a use for in the classroom. It also makes me think of the kind of descriptive writing that a scene like this would deserve, a barren landscape suddenly turned to colour.

There is also solid, measurable conservation news from northern Spain. Good News Network reports that the Cantabrian brown bear population has roughly doubled over the last twenty years, from as few as one hundred and forty animals to about three hundred and seventy. The bears are also now ranging over a much wider area than before. I like stories like this because they are concrete. There are numbers, there is a timescale, and there is a clear outcome. Twenty years is a long time to keep faith with a project, and it is encouraging to see the figures rise so clearly.

And then something more imaginative from Reasons to be Cheerful, co-published with the Outrider Foundation. The piece imagines the mossy cities of the future, and it centres on Philip Wallisfurth, who in twenty twelve proposed using moss to save a hundred-and-fifty-year-old tree in Aachen. From that one idea, the article sketches a vision of greener, softer cities, where moss is part of the urban fabric rather than something to be scraped away. I will not claim more about the details than the piece offers, but it is a gentle and inventive thought. If you picture the old stone walls of a town covered in a velvet green, it is a rather poetic image too.

Finally, two stories about people, which I think are the heart of this briefing.

The first is from Good News Network, and it is about Bonnie Fay, an eighty-four-year-old piano player in Pennsylvania. She has returned to the Bryn Mawr Village nursing home, where she was once a patient after being struck down by Guillain-Barré syndrome. Now she goes back to give music to the residents. The headline speaks of paralysis not stopping her and of her making good on a musical promise. There is something very moving about that: someone who was once cared for in that place coming back to play, and in doing so giving something back. It is a story of recovery and generosity, and of course it has music at its centre. I imagine the sound of a piano in a nursing-home common room, and I find it hard not to smile.

The second is from The Optimist Daily, part of its Local Changemakers twenty twenty-six series. It is about Prince Bashangezi, a former A-Level student at Tongogara Refugee Camp in Zimbabwe. When COVID lockdowns took away his schooling, he took that loss and turned it into peer tutoring for other refugee students. As a teacher yourself, I think you will appreciate this one. It is a reminder that education is something people pass on to one another, sometimes in the most difficult circumstances, and that a student who has lost something can become the very person who helps others to keep going. It is also, I notice, an A-Level story, which brings it rather close to your own classroom.

So that is the picture for the last two days: a record-breaking writer, a forgotten adventurer credited at last, hidden art and hidden coins, a desert in flower, bears returning to the mountains, and two people who answered difficulty with generosity. If you can, I hope you will take a slow walk up in Belledonne today and enjoy a bit of that quiet optimism for yourself.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle couple of days for watching, with a great deal of ballet, some lovely ARTE documentaries, and a Netflix thriller or two if you fancy something to bite into.

Let me begin with the Royal Ballet and Opera, who have put out a cluster of videos on YouTube. The two I'd point you to first are both from Kenneth MacMillan's Requiem, set to Fauré. It was made as an elegy for John Cranko, and the Sanctus in particular is described as a luminous, grief-laden ensemble piece, created for Stuttgart Ballet after Cranko's death. The Libera me comes from the same work, and it's a meditation on grief and consolation. Together they would suit a quiet morning very well, with a cup of something warm and the mountains outside your window.

There is also something to look forward to. The Royal Ballet has released a trailer for MADDADDAM, a new work by Wayne McGregor based on Margaret Atwood's dystopian trilogy, with an original score by Max Richter. It runs at the Royal Opera House in London from the twenty-second of February to the thirteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven. With your fondness for Atwood and for dance, it's a rather tempting meeting of the two, and the trailer gives a first taste of how a novelist's imagined world might be translated into movement.

If you'd like something more traditional, the company has also posted a trailer for Liam Scarlett's Swan Lake. It's set to Tchaikovsky, with designs by John Macfarlane, and tells the story of Odette, the cursed princess, and Siegfried. It's a good doorway into classical ballet, though no date or platform is given beyond the video itself.

And for a literary angle, there is an introduction to the Royal Opera's Carmen, in Damiano Michieletto's production, which is set in the heat of Spain. What will interest you is that it talks about how Bizet's opera draws on Prosper Mérimée's novella. It's a nice example of a story travelling from page to stage, and perhaps useful if you ever want to show pupils how one text can be reshaped in another art form.

Staying with music, The Guardian reviews a concert by the BBC Symphony Orchestra at the Barbican Hall in London. Sakari Oramo conducted, and the Korean violinist Inmo Yang played Bartók. The critic calls Yang phenomenal, but says the orchestra shone even brighter on the night, which is a lovely thing to read about a band that is so often taken for granted.

Now to ARTE, where there are three items worth knowing about. The first is a documentary on Victor Horta and the birth of Art nouveau. It begins with the opening of the Hôtel Tassel in Brussels in eighteen ninety-three, and follows Horta's use of iron, glass and light, and then the way the movement spread across Europe. Given your love of the links between the visual arts and literature, and of the Belle Époque in particular, this feels made for you.

The second is an ARTE reportage called Israël : le siècle de Nelly. It follows Nelly, a Holocaust survivor whose childhood was in Pacov, in the Czech Republic, and whose long life spans the early years of the State of Israel. It's a personal account of history, the sort of lived story that often teaches more than a textbook can, and it will no doubt be a weighty watch, so one for when you have the time and the quiet.

The third is lighter in subject but not in thought. It's an episode of Les idées larges, with the sociologist Baptiste Coulmont, asking whether our first names really belong to us. He uses what they reveal about French society and its history to show how a small, everyday matter can illuminate wider social change. As someone who spends her days thinking about characters and what we call them, you may enjoy it.

Two items touch on dance in a different key. The Times Union writes about a film called Living in the Grey, which explores dance after brain injury. I only have the headline, and no platform is named, so I can't tell you where to find it, but it's a dance documentary and so worth keeping an eye out for. And, more lightly, there's a piece about a new Barbie-themed Nutcracker, where dancers are pausing it to check whether the footwork is accurate. It's from a site called Startefacts, and again I don't know the platform, but it's a fun little item for anyone who has ever looked at a pair of feet on stage and felt very strongly about them.

Finally, for the evenings when you want a thriller, Netflix is busy. The headline show is The Body, a new eight-part psychological thriller. Collider's review calls it unlike anything else currently streaming, and ScreenRant describes it as the perfect binge for this week. A third ScreenRant piece reports that a new eight-part Netflix psychological thriller has earned a rare perfect score on Rotten Tomatoes. It seems very likely to be the same series, though the text is thin, so I'd treat that as probable rather than certain. I can't tell you the verdict of the Collider review beyond that, but the overall mood is one of real enthusiasm.

There's also a separate item from MovieWeb about a new six-part crime thriller on Netflix, which it says is taking over on streaming. All I have is the headline, so I don't know the title, the premise or the cast, but it may be worth a glance on the app if you like your drama tense and plot-driven.

Enjoy the choosing, Yamuna, and I hope something here makes your evening a little more beautiful.

Good morning, Yamuna. It's a gentle, slightly grey Thursday, and the last two days have brought a good mix of Netflix thrillers, a generous helping of Royal Ballet and Opera films, and some thoughtful viewing on ARTE.

I should be honest that the extracts I have are brief, so I can't tell you the premise, the cast or the critic's fuller verdict. But the word "unlike" is interesting. When a critic says a series is unlike anything else on streaming, it usually means it is doing something with its form or its atmosphere, not just following a formula. ScreenRant also has an item about a new eight-part Netflix psychological thriller that has earned a rare perfect score on Rotten Tomatoes. It doesn't name the series in the text I have, but the description matches The Body closely, so it may well be the same show. There is also a second, separate Netflix item. MovieWeb reports that Netflix has found a new six-part crime thriller hit, and says it is officially taking over on streaming. All I have is the headline, so I can't give you the story, the setting or who is in it. But six episodes is a pleasingly compact length. If the eight-part psychological thriller feels like too large a commitment, this could be the shorter option for a quiet evening in Les Adrets. I'd treat both as things to keep an eye on rather than things to rush towards, until a little more is said about what they actually are.

Now to the part of the day that I think will be most to your taste, which is the Royal Ballet and Opera material. The company has put a cluster of videos on its YouTube channel, and together they make a lovely little programme.

A novel built on a strong, unsettling imagined world, a choreographer known for pushing the body into new shapes, and a composer whose music so often sits between the classical and the contemporary: it is an interesting meeting of talents. A trailer can only tell you so much, but it is a good way to see how the company plans to translate the page to the stage. They also sit nicely next to each other. You could watch them as a pair, one after the other, and let the music carry you.

For something lighter and more theatrical, there are two more from the same channel. Staying with dance, there are two smaller items from the press. The Times Union writes about a film called Living in the Grey, which explores dance after brain injury. All I have is the headline, so I can't tell you where to see it or how it is made. But the subject is striking, and it falls into one of your favourite categories, the dance documentary. It is a playful piece, and it won't be essential viewing, but it is a nice reminder that people who know a craft deeply will always watch with a very particular kind of attention. The platform isn't stated, so I can't say where you would find it.

On the concert side, The Guardian has a review of the BBC Symphony Orchestra at the Barbican Hall in London, with Sakari Oramo conducting and the Korean violinist Inmo Yang playing Bartók. The headline says that yes, Inmo Yang is phenomenal, but the BBC Symphony shone even brighter. It is a lovely sentence, because it praises a brilliant soloist and then says the orchestra surpassed even that. I don't have the details of how the evening unfolded, but it is the sort of review that makes you wish you had been in the hall. If you are curious, it is a good one to read with some Bartók playing in the background.

Finally, ARTE, which gave you three quite different pieces, all on the ARTE Concert channel on YouTube.

The one I would single out for you is the documentary on Victor Horta and the birth of Art nouveau. It begins in eighteen ninety-three, with the opening of the Hôtel Tassel in Brussels, and follows Horta's use of iron, glass and light. It then traces how the movement spread across Europe. Given how much you love the connections between painting, architecture and literature, and your interest in the Belle Époque, I think this will feel like a natural fit. There is something very literary about Art nouveau, with its curving lines that look almost like handwriting or the tendrils of a plant, and a film that starts from one single house and opens outwards to a whole movement is a pleasing way to tell it.

The second is an ARTE reportage called Israël: le siècle de Nelly. It follows Nelly, a Holocaust survivor whose childhood was in Pacov, in the Czech Republic, and whose life spans the early years of the State of Israel. You often value that kind of testimony, where history is learned through a person and not a textbook, in the way a good novel can do. It is likely to be a serious watch, so perhaps one for a quieter moment.

The third is a more everyday subject, but a thoughtful one. In an episode of Les idées larges, the sociologist Baptiste Coulmont asks whether our first name belongs to us. The programme looks at what first names reveal about French society and its history. It takes a small, familiar thing and uses it to show how society has changed. For someone who spends her days with fictional characters, whose names are so carefully chosen, it might be quite a charming way to think about how real names carry meaning too.

So, there is plenty to choose from, and very little of it needs your full attention at once. Enjoy whichever one calls to you first, Yamuna.

briefing.text:
Good morning, Yamuna, and happy Thursday.

Let me start close to home. This Saturday, the fourteenth of November, there's an organ concert of Bach at the Saint-Joseph church in Grenoble, reported by Le Dauphiné Libéré. It's a lovely excuse for a Saturday outing, with all that counterpoint filling a stone nave. Over in Chambéry, there's an exhibition of Albanian portraits, the "icons" that a dictatorship tried to erase, as Unidivers puts it. The write-up is brief, but the idea is a strong one: history told through faces that someone once wanted gone.

Now some good news. Researchers in Spain have found two hundred and eighty Ice Age engravings in a cave on the Mediterranean coast. It's the third-largest collection of its kind found there, and visitors had been walking past them for more than sixty years without noticing. Good News Network calls it prehistoric art hidden in plain sight, which is rather humbling for the rest of us. And from Pennsylvania, a gentler story. Bonnie Fay, who is eighty-four and plays the piano, has gone back to the Bryn Mawr Village nursing home, where she once stayed as a patient with Guillain-Barré syndrome. She's there to give music back to the residents who are there now. It's a small, warm tale of recovery and generosity.

On to books, and it's a busy day. M. John Harrison has won the 2026 Booker Prize with The End of Everything, and at eighty-one he becomes the oldest winner of the prize for fiction. The Conversation has an essay calling the novel a wonder of weird fiction for our incomprehensible times, and it reads the book as writing that speaks to its moment. If you like strange narrators and fiction that catches the strangeness of the present, this may be one for your list.

Also in the Guardian, there's a review of Jane Schoenbrun's first novel, Public Access Afterworld. Its narrator is Bethany Peters, a trans content moderator at a company much like YouTube, who spends her days watching disturbing material. The reviewer calls it a wry, fun descent into the dark world behind our screens, and it sounds as if the voice is what carries it.

Over at Literary Hub, Adam Gopnik revisits Hemingway's The Sun Also Rises, a hundred years on. He weighs the prejudices that have dated badly against whatever it is that still holds readers, and asks how a novel ages and why some of them do it better than others. It strikes me as a ready-made conversation for a classroom.

And two notes for the BFI corner. The BBC has an inside story of how Ian Charleson played Hamlet on stage while he was dying of Aids. It's a moving account of what happens when a role takes on personal weight, and it speaks directly to the Hamlet on the 2027 syllabus. Then, rather more lightly, Florida Weekly has a short piece on love and deception in Sheridan's The Rivals. It's brief, but a reminder that this comedy is a 2027 text, and a handy one for a seconde or première class.

Now, where words meet paint. In Paris, at the Théâtre Montparnasse, the great Catherine Hiegel is bringing the painter Suzanne Valadon back to life in a play set in nineteen thirty-five, three years before Valadon's death. Beaux Arts Magazine has the story, and it's a nice meeting of the studio and the stage.

Hyperallergic reviews a new documentary on the collage artist Romare Bearden. The reviewer finds the best moments are those in which we simply watch people engaging with his work, which feels about right for an artist whose pictures are built from fragments.

And the National Gallery has published a three-part film series today, called Linked Lives: Art and Empire. It looks at how the gallery's early history was shaped by empire and colonialism, drawing on Dr Sean Cham's research into the lives behind the paintings, including enslaved people so often left out of institutional history. It's the sort of thing that changes how you see a wall of famous canvases.

Two things to look forward to on screen and stage. ARTE has a documentary on Victor Horta and the birth of Art nouveau. It begins with the opening of the Hôtel Tassel in Brussels in eighteen ninety-three, and follows his use of iron, glass and light as the movement spread across Europe. And the Royal Ballet has released a trailer for MADDADDAM, Wayne McGregor's ballet based on Margaret Atwood's dystopian trilogy, with an original score by Max Richter. It runs at the Royal Opera House in London from the twenty-second of February to the thirteenth of March, twenty twenty-seven. Atwood, dance and Richter in one evening does seem made for you.

To finish, two bits of France. The Guardian has dug out an archive piece from the eleventh of November, nineteen seventy-six, in which five British chefs cook a lunch at Maxim's in Paris, in the long-running contest between British and French cooking. Apparently it's witty, richly written, and a window onto a vanished dining world. And The Local France has the French expression of the day: "Tu parles !" It isn't a plain statement of the obvious but a retort that signals scepticism or irony, rather like our "Yeah, right." Handy for a teacher of English whose pupils live between two idioms.

That's your Thursday, Yamuna. I hope it's a gentle one, and that somewhere in it you find a bit of Bach.
